title: Quantifying Mixed-state Entanglement Via Partial Transpose And Realignment Moments
authors: Poetri Sonya Tarabunga And Tobias Haug
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2194 (2026).

Entanglement plays a crucial role in quantum information science and many-body physics, yet quantifying it in mixed quantum many-body systems has remained a notoriously difficult problem. Here, we introduce families of quantitative entanglement witnesses, constructed from partial transpose and realignment moments, which provide rigorous bounds on entanglement monotones as well as entanglement dimensionality. Our witnesses can be efficiently measured using SWAP tests or variants of Bell measurements, thus making them directly implementable on current hardware. Leveraging our witnesses, we present several novel results on entanglement properties of mixed states, both in quantum information and many-body physics. We develop efficient algorithms to test whether mixed states with bounded entropy have low or high entanglement, which previously was only possible for pure states. We also provide an efficient algorithm to test the Schmidt rank using only two-copy measurements, and the operator Schmidt rank using four-copy measurements. Further, our witnesses robustly certify the quantum circuit depth in the presence of noise, as well as the Schmidt rank of mixed states. Finally, we show that the entanglement phase diagram of Haar random states, quantified by the partial transpose negativity, can be fully established solely by computing our witness, a result that also applies to any state [MATH]-design. Our witnesses can also be efficiently computed for matrix product states, thus enabling the characterization of entanglement in extensive many-body systems. Finally, we make progress on the entanglement required for quantum cryptography, establishing rigorous limits on pseudoentanglement and pseudorandom density matrices with bounded entropy. Our work opens new avenues for quantifying entanglement in large and noisy quantum systems.

.
tldr: This paper introduces new entanglement witnesses based on partial transpose and realignment moments to efficiently quantify mixed-state entanglement and dimensionality.
motivation: Quantifying entanglement in mixed quantum many-body systems is notoriously difficult, and existing methods often require pure states or are inefficient for large noisy systems.
method: The authors construct entanglement witnesses from moments of partial transpose and realignment, measurable via SWAP tests or Bell measurements, and develop algorithms for testing entanglement, Schmidt rank, and circuit depth.
result: The witnesses provide rigorous bounds on entanglement monotones and dimensionality, enable efficient certification of mixed states with bounded entropy, and characterize entanglement phase diagrams of Haar random states.
conclusion: The work offers practical tools for quantifying entanglement in large and noisy quantum systems, with applications in many-body physics and quantum cryptography.

title: Measurement Incompatibility In Bayesian Multiparameter Quantum Estimation
authors: Francesco Albarelli, Dominic Branford, And Jesús Rubio
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2192 (2026).

We present a comprehensive and pedagogical formulation of Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation. Within this framework, we analyse the role of measurement incompatibility and establish its quantitative effect on attainable precision. We achieve this by deriving upper bounds based on the pretty good measurement – a notion from hypothesis testing – combined with the evaluation of the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound. In general, we prove that, as in the many-copy regime of local estimation theory, incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss relative to the idealised scenario in which individually optimal measurements are assumed jointly implementable. Therefore, in practical situations, the latter may provide a sufficient and computationally efficient benchmark without solving the full optimisation problem. Our results, which we illustrate through applications of discrete phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing, provide analytical and numerical tools for assessing ultimate precision limits and the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology, including an open-source package for all the bounds discussed here.

.
tldr: This paper provides a comprehensive Bayesian framework for multiparameter quantum estimation, quantifying the impact of measurement incompatibility on precision and deriving tight bounds using pretty good measurements and Nagaoka-Hayashi bounds.
motivation: Bayesian multiparameter estimation is crucial for quantum metrology, but measurement incompatibility can degrade precision. Existing results often focus on asymptotic limits, leaving a gap for finite-sample and practical scenarios.
method: The authors formulate Bayesian multiparameter estimation and derive upper bounds based on the pretty good measurement, along with the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound. They also provide an open-source package for numerical evaluation.
result: They prove that measurement incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss compared to the idealized scenario with jointly implementable optimal measurements, even in practical situations. Applications to phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing demonstrate the tools.
conclusion: The work offers analytical and numerical tools for assessing ultimate precision limits in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology, showing that the idealized benchmark is often sufficient, thus simplifying optimization.

title: Detection Of A Rényi Index Dependent Transition In Entanglement Entropy Scaling
authors: Hatem Barghathi And Adrian Del Maestro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2184 (2026).

The scaling of entanglement with subsystem size encodes key information about phases and criticality, but the von Neumann entropy is costly to access in experiments and simulations, often requiring full state tomography. The second Rényi entropy is readily measured using two-copy protocols and is often used as a proxy for the von Neumann entanglement entropy, where it is assumed to track its asymptotic scaling. Sugino and Korepiny (Int. J. Mod. Phys. B 32, 1850306 (2018)) revealed that in the ground state of some highly constrained spin models, the scaling of the von Neumann and Rényi entropies can differ, varying from power law to logarithmic scaling as a function of the Rényi index. Here, we construct a number-conserving many-body state that demonstrates a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, generalizing previous results to the case of interacting fermions. We introduce a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy built from charge-resolved Rényi entropies that can provide a protocol for diagnosing anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.

.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a Rényi-index-dependent transition in entanglement entropy scaling for interacting fermions and introduces a symmetry-aware lower bound to diagnose such anomalous scaling from experimentally accessible data.
motivation: The von Neumann entropy is difficult to measure, so the second Rényi entropy is often used as a proxy, but they can have different scaling in constrained systems. This paper aims to understand and detect such differences.
method: The authors construct a number-conserving many-body state of interacting fermions and analyze the scaling of Rényi entropies for various index values. They introduce a lower bound on the von Neumann entropy using charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
result: They observe a change in the leading scaling exponent with the Rényi index, generalizing previous results to fermionic systems, and propose a diagnostic protocol based on the lower bound.
conclusion: The symmetry-aware lower bound provides a practical way to detect anomalous entanglement scaling from experimental data, even when direct von Neumann entropy measurement is infeasible.

title: Entanglement Growth In The Dark Intervals Of A Locally Monitored Free-fermion Chain
authors: Giovanni Di Fresco, Youenn Le Gal, Davide Valenti, Marco Schiró, And Angelo Carollo
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2183 (2026).

We consider a free fermionic chain with monitoring of the particle density on a single site of the chain and study the entanglement dynamics of quantum jump trajectories. We show that the entanglement entropy grows in time towards a stationary state which display volume law scaling of the entropy, in stark contrast with both the unitary dynamics after a local quench and the no-click limit corresponding to full post-selection. We explain the extensive entanglement growth as a consequence of the peculiar distribution of quantum jumps in time, which display superpoissonian waiting time distribution characterised by a bunching of quantum jumps followed by long dark intervals where no-clicks are detected, akin to the distribution of fluorescence light in a driven atom. We show that the presence of dark intervals is the key feature to explain the effect and that by increasing the number of sites which are monitored the volume law scaling gives away to the Zeno effect and its associated area law.

.
tldr: This paper shows that local monitoring of a free-fermion chain leads to extensive entanglement growth with volume law scaling, explained by super-Poissonian quantum jump distributions and dark intervals.
motivation: Understanding how measurement-induced dynamics affect entanglement in many-body quantum systems is crucial for quantum information processing and foundational questions about quantum measurement.
method: The authors study a free-fermion chain with a single-site density monitoring, analyzing quantum jump trajectories and computing the entanglement entropy of the quantum state conditioned on the measurement record.
result: They find that the entanglement entropy grows to a stationary state with volume law scaling, in contrast to unitary dynamics and the no-click limit, and attribute this to bunching of quantum jumps followed by long dark intervals. Increasing the number of monitored sites leads to area law via the Zeno effect.
conclusion: The presence of dark intervals in the jump statistics is the key mechanism for extensive entanglement growth, providing insight into measurement-induced phase transitions and the role of monitoring in quantum systems.

title: Quantum Nonlocality Without Entanglement And State Discrimination Measures
authors: Shayeef Murshid, Tathagata Gupta, Vincent Russo, And Somshubhro Bandyopadhyay
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2174 (2026).

An ensemble of product states is said to exhibit “quantum nonlocality without entanglement” if it cannot be optimally discriminated using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). We show that this property can depend on the chosen discrimination measure. Specifically, we construct a family of ensembles, each consisting of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states, for which LOCC fails to achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but succeeds in achieving optimal unambiguous discrimination. We further extend our construction to multipartite systems and provide strong numerical evidence that a similar separation between local and global optima is present for minimum-error discrimination, but not for unambiguous discrimination.

.
tldr: The paper demonstrates that quantum nonlocality without entanglement depends on the chosen discrimination measure by constructing product-state ensembles where LOCC fails for minimum-error but succeeds for unambiguous discrimination.
motivation: To investigate how the phenomenon of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is affected by the operational task of state discrimination, potentially revealing measure-dependent aspects.
method: The authors explicitly construct families of bipartite ensembles of six linearly independent product states and extend them to multipartite systems, analyzing LOCC discrimination for both minimum-error and unambiguous measures, supplemented by numerical evidence.
result: They find a separation between local and global optima for minimum-error discrimination but not for unambiguous discrimination, indicating a dependence on the discrimination measure.
conclusion: The property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is not an intrinsic property but depends on the discrimination measure used, highlighting the nuanced nature of LOCC constraints.

title: Complete Discrimination Of D -dimensional ...
authors: Wen-Qiang Liu And Hai-Rui Wei Jun-Hai Zhao
abstract: The indefinite causal order (ICO) has been recognized as a novel resource for applications in specific quantum information processing tasks due to its intriguing advantages. We propose a set of schemes to completely and deterministically discriminate -dimensional -partite Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) states via ICO structure, and then we develop a set of architectures for implementing these schemes in the gravity fields. Based on the geometry configuration of the gravitational quantum switch, a set of orthogonal GHZ states can be classified into groups. The orthogonal states in each group can be further easily distinguished by discriminating their qudit information in the basis . Compared with previous protocols, our schemes greatly simplify the discrimination process, and additional GHZ states, conditional controlled gates, or platforms are not required. Note that the nondestructive -dimensional -partite GHZ-state analysis can also be achieved by iterating the gravitational quantum switch for two rounds as the ICO structure is not consumed in the construction process. Our results hold significant implications for quantum communication and the interdisciplinary field of quantum information and quantum gravity.
tldr: The paper proposes schemes using indefinite causal order to completely discriminate multi-partite GHZ states deterministically and implements them via gravitational quantum switches.
motivation: GHZ state discrimination is important for quantum communication, and existing methods require complex resources; the authors aim to simplify using ICO.
method: They use the structure of indefinite causal order (gravitational quantum switch) to classify GHZ states into groups, then perform discrimination via qudit measurements.
result: They achieve complete deterministic discrimination of D-dimensional N-partite GHZ states without additional GHZ states or conditional gates, and can also realize non-destructive analysis.
conclusion: The approach simplifies discrimination and has implications for quantum communication and quantum gravity.

title: Quantum Measurement Of Work In Mesoscopic Systems
authors: Anant Vijay Varma And Doron Cohen
abstract: Heat and work in thermodynamics refer to the measurement of changes in energy content of external bodies (baths and agents). We discuss the implications of quantum mechanics on the possibility to measure work in the mesoscopic context. The agent is a quantum entity (say an oscillator) that is used to drive the system. An inherent limitation is related to back-reaction, leading to a classical-like restriction. We find that in order to resolve fingerprints of interference, an additional quantum uncertainty limitation should be taken into account in the design of the agent. This quantum limitation is fundamental, not merely noise-like blurring.
tldr: This paper examines fundamental quantum limitations on measuring work in mesoscopic systems driven by a quantum agent, identifying a quantum uncertainty constraint beyond classical back-reaction.
motivation: To understand how quantum mechanics restricts the measurability of work in mesoscopic thermodynamic contexts, particularly when the driving agent is itself a quantum entity.
method: The authors model the agent as a quantum oscillator driving the system and analyze the effects of back-reaction and quantum uncertainty on work measurement, possibly using theoretical frameworks for quantum measurement and thermodynamics.
result: They find that resolving interference fingerprints in work distributions requires accounting for an additional quantum uncertainty limitation, which is fundamental rather than noise-like.
conclusion: The quantum measurement of work in mesoscopic systems is fundamentally constrained by both back-reaction and a deeper quantum uncertainty, which must be incorporated in agent design.

title: Robust Topological Quantum State Transfer With Long-range Interactions In Rydberg Arrays
authors: Siri Raupach, Beatriz Olmos, And Mathias B. M. Svendsen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2190 (2026).

We develop a theoretical framework for fast, robust and high-fidelity topological quantum state transfer in one-dimensional systems with long-range couplings, motivated by chains of Rydberg atoms with dipole–dipole interactions. Such long-range interactions naturally give rise to extended Su–Schrieffer–Heeger and Rice–Mele models supporting topologically protected edge states. We show that these edge states enable high-fidelity edge-to-edge excitation transfer using both time-independent protocols, based on coherent edge state dynamics, and time-dependent protocols, based on adiabatic modulation of system parameters. Long-range couplings play a central role by enhancing the relevant energy gaps, leading to a substantial improvement in transfer efficiency compared to nearest neighbour models. The resulting transfer is robust against positional disorder, reflecting its topological origin and highlighting the potential of long-range interacting platforms for reliable quantum state transfer.

.
tldr: This paper presents a theoretical framework for fast, robust, and high-fidelity topological quantum state transfer in long-range interacting Rydberg arrays, showing that long-range couplings enhance energy gaps and improve transfer efficiency compared to nearest-neighbor models.
motivation: State transfer is crucial for quantum information processing, but it is often limited by short-range interactions and disorder. The authors aim to leverage topological protection and long-range couplings in Rydberg arrays to achieve reliable transfer.
method: The study models one-dimensional systems with dipole-dipole interactions, leading to extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger and Rice-Mele models with topologically protected edge states. Both time-independent and time-dependent (adiabatic) protocols are analyzed to transfer excitations between edges.
result: Long-range couplings significantly enhance the relevant energy gaps, leading to substantially higher transfer efficiency compared to nearest-neighbor models, and the transfer remains robust against positional disorder due to topological protection.
conclusion: The work highlights the potential of long-range interacting platforms, such as Rydberg arrays, for implementing fast and robust quantum state transfer, which is relevant for scalable quantum information processing.

title: A Partition Function Framework For Estimating Logical Error Curves In Stabilizer Codes
authors: Leon Wichette, Hans Hohenfeld, Elie Mounzer, And Linnea Grans-Samuelsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2175 (2026).

Based on the mapping between stabilizer quantum error correcting codes and disordered statistical mechanics models, we define a ratio of partition functions that measures the success probability for maximum partition function decoding, which at the Nishimori temperature corresponds to maximum likelihood (ML) decoding. We show that this ratio differs from the similarly defined order probability and describe the decoding strategy whose success rate is described by the order probability. We refer to the latter as a probabilistic partition function decoding and show that it is the strategy that at zero temperature corresponds to maximum probability (MP) decoding. Based on the difference between the two decoders, we discuss the possibility of a maximum partition function decodability boundary outside the order-disorder phase boundary. At zero temperature, the difference between the two ratios measures to what degree MP decoding can be improved by accounting for degeneracy among maximum probability errors, through methods such as ensembling. We consider in detail the example of the toric code under bitflip noise, which maps to the Random Bond Ising Model. We demonstrate that estimation of logical performance through decoding probability and order probability is more sample efficient than estimation by counting failures of the corresponding decoders, especially in the regime of low noise. We consider both uniform noise and noise where qubits are given individual error rates. The latter noise model lifts the degeneracy among maximum probability errors, but we show that ensembling remains useful as long as it also samples less probable errors. We also consider, in less detail, the color code under bitflip and depolarizing noise.

.
tldr: 该论文提出了一个基于配分函数的框架，用于估计稳定子码的逻辑错误率，并应用于toric码。
motivation: 需要高效且可靠的方法来评估量子纠错码的性能，特别是逻辑错误率与噪声参数的关系。
method: 利用稳定子码到无序统计力学模型的映射，定义配分函数比值来衡量最大配分函数解码的成功概率，并区分最大似然解码和最大概率解码。
result: 在toric码和比特翻转噪声下，证明了估计解码概率和有序概率比直接计数解码失败更有效，且讨论了简并性和集成方法的作用。
conclusion: 该框架提供了一种新的视角来分析和估计量子纠错码的性能，有助于理解解码策略和错误抑制。

title: A Complete Theory Of The Clifford Commutant
authors: Lennart Bittel, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone, Antonio A. Mele, And Salvatore F.E. Oliviero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2171 (2026).

The Clifford group plays a central role in quantum information science. It is the building block for many error-correcting schemes and matches the first three moments of the Haar measure over the unitary group-a property that is essential for a broad range of quantum algorithms, with applications in pseudorandomness, learning theory, benchmarking, and entanglement distillation. At the heart of understanding many properties of the Clifford group lies the Clifford commutant: the set of operators that commute with [MATH]-fold tensor powers of Clifford unitaries. Previous understanding of this commutant has been limited to relatively small values of [MATH], constrained by the number of qubits [MATH]. In this work, we develop a complete theory of the Clifford commutant. Our first result provides an explicit orthogonal basis for the commutant and computes its dimension for arbitrary [MATH] and [MATH]. We also introduce an alternative and easy-to-manipulate basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. We show that this basis is generated by products of permutations, which generate the unitary group commutant, and at most three other operators. Additionally, we develop a graphical calculus allowing a diagrammatic manipulation of elements of this basis. These results enable a wealth of applications: among others, we characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, whose success probability also offers an operational interpretation to stabilizer entropies. Finally, we show that these results also generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

.
tldr: A complete theory of the Clifford commutant is developed, including explicit bases and applications to magic measures and stabilizer property testing.
motivation: The Clifford commutant was only understood for small parameters; a full characterization for arbitrary numbers of qubits and copies is needed for many quantum information applications.
method: An orthogonal basis for the commutant is constructed, along with an alternative basis using isotropic sums of Pauli operators, and a graphical calculus is introduced.
result: The dimension of the commutant is computed for arbitrary parameters, the generating structure is identified, and applications to magic measures and optimal stabilizer testing are demonstrated.
conclusion: This work provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for the Clifford commutant, with implications for quantum resource theories and property testing.

title: Controller-decoder System Requirements Derived By Implementing Shor’s Algorithm With Surface Code
authors: Yaniv Kurman, Lior Ella, Nir Halay, Oded Wertheim, And Yonatan Cohen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2170 (2026).

Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is regarded as the most promising path to quantum advantage. The success of QEC relies on achieving quantum gate fidelities below the error threshold of the QEC code, while accurately decoding errors through classical processing of the QEC stabilizer measurements. In this paper, we uncover the critical system-level requirements from a controller-decoder system (CDS) necessary to successfully execute the next milestone in QEC: a non-Clifford circuit. Using a representative non-Clifford circuit, of Shor factorization algorithm for the number 21, we convert the logical-level circuit to a QEC surface code circuit and finally to the physical level circuit. By taking into account realistic implementation aspects using typical superconducting qubit processor parameters, we reveal a broad range of core requirements from any CDS aimed at performing error corrected quantum computation. Our findings indicate that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must remain within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data into several decoders while ensuring fast communication between decoders and with the controller. By extending existing simulation techniques, we simulate the complete fault-tolerant factorization circuit at the physical level, demonstrating that near-term hardware performance in the scale of 0.1% physical error rates and 1000 qubits, are sufficient for a successful circuit execution. Overall, the requirements outlined here set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

A video of the physical-level gate sequences for the factorization circuit with distance-3 surfaces. (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17970554)

.
tldr: This paper derives system-level requirements for a controller-decoder system to execute non-Clifford circuits in surface code quantum error correction, using Shor's algorithm for factoring 21 as a benchmark, and shows that near-term hardware with 0.1% error rates and 1000 qubits suffices.
motivation: Quantum error correction is the path to quantum advantage, but executing non-Clifford circuits requires specific decoding and control capabilities. The authors aim to identify the critical requirements for a controller-decoder system (CDS) to successfully run a non-Clifford circuit.
method: They convert a logical-level Shor's algorithm circuit for factoring 21 into a surface code circuit and then to a physical-level circuit, considering realistic superconducting qubit parameters. They extend existing simulation techniques to simulate the entire fault-tolerant circuit at the physical level, analyzing the CDS latency and decoding requirements.
result: They find that the CDS closed-loop latency must be within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data across multiple decoders with fast communication. They demonstrate that near-term hardware with ~0.1% physical error rates and ~1000 qubits can successfully execute the circuit.
conclusion: The outlined requirements provide guidance for near- and medium-term experimental implementations of non-Clifford QEC circuits, highlighting the need for efficient decoder architectures and control systems.

title: Simple Logical Quantum Computation With Concatenated Symplectic Double Codes
authors: Noah Berthusen And Elijah Durso-Sabina
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2195 (2026).

There have been significant recent advances in constructing theoretical and practical quantum error correcting codes that function well as quantum memories; however, performing fault-tolerant logical gates on these codes is less studied, and the protocols that do exist often require significant complexity. Building off the symplectic double construction, we investigate concatenated symplectic double codes, which have a rich set of logical gates implementable using only physical single-qubit gates and qubit relabeling. Combined with injected fold-transversal gates, the full Clifford group on a single codeblock is achieved through a functionally simple circuit. We perform circuit-level simulations of state preparation and quantum error correction on these codes and show that they have promising performance at near state-of-the-art physical error rates. As such, we argue that concatenated symplectic double codes are strong contenders as the underlying computational code on medium- to large-scale quantum computers.

.
tldr: Concatenated symplectic double codes enable simple fault-tolerant logical gates using only physical single-qubit gates and qubit relabeling, with promising simulated performance.
motivation: Existing fault-tolerant logical gate protocols for quantum error correcting codes are often complex; this work seeks simpler methods.
method: The authors build on symplectic double codes and concatenation, combine with injected fold-transversal gates to achieve the full Clifford group, and perform circuit-level simulations of state preparation and error correction.
result: Simulations show promising performance at near state-of-the-art physical error rates, indicating these codes are competitive for practical quantum computing.
conclusion: Concatenated symplectic double codes are strong candidates for the underlying computational code on medium- to large-scale quantum computers.

title: Catalytic $z$-rotations In Constant $T$-depth
authors: Isaac H. Kim
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2191 (2026).

We show that the [MATH]-depth of any single-qubit [MATH]-rotation can be reduced to [MATH] if a certain catalyst state is available. To achieve an [MATH]-approximation, it suffices to have a catalyst state of size polynomial in [MATH]. This implies that [MATH] admits a finite universal gate set consisting of Clifford+[MATH]. In particular, there are catalytic constant [MATH]-depth circuits that approximate multi-qubit Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform arbitrarily well. We also show that the catalyst state can be prepared in time polynomial in [MATH].

.
tldr: The paper demonstrates that any single-qubit z-rotation can be performed in constant T-depth using a catalytic state of polynomial size, enabling constant-depth approximations of multi-qubit gates with Clifford+T.
motivation: T gates are costly in fault-tolerant quantum computing, and reducing T-depth is crucial. The authors aim to overcome the lower bound on T-depth for exact rotations by employing catalysis.
method: They identify a specific catalyst state and show that with it, any z-rotation can be approximated with T-depth 1. They analyze the required catalyst size as a function of the approximation error.
result: A catalyst of size polynomial in the desired error suffices for arbitrarily good approximations. This leads to constant T-depth circuits for multi-qubit Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform.
conclusion: The existence of catalytic constant-depth circuits implies that Clifford+T is a universal gate set with constant T-depth for many operations, potentially reducing the overhead of magic state distillation.

title: Entanglement-assisted Quasi-cyclic Quantum Low-density Parity-check Codes Over Qubits
authors: Pavan Kumar, Abhi Kumar Sharma, Karthik Bharadwaj, And Shayan Srinivasa Garani
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2181 (2026).

We construct several families of entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC (EA-QC-QLDPC) codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices. The entanglement-unassisted portion of the joint Tanner graph of the proposed EA-QC-QLDPC code derived from two distinct classical QC-LDPC codes is free of 4-cycles. Notably, one of the proposed families constructed from two distinct classical codes requires only a [MATH] shared Bell pair between the quantum transmitter and receiver, highlighting its resource efficiency. We also analytically determine the exact code rates for some of the proposed constructions. Furthermore, two of the proposed families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes are derived from a single classical code whose Tanner graphs possess girth greater than six, further enhancing their error-correcting performance. We also propose an encoding scheme with improved complexity by exploiting the proposed code structure. The performance of the proposed codes is assessed under both random and burst error models under the depolarizing and Markovian noise actions. Simulation results reveal nearly one order of improvement in error-correction performance with the quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum (QBLNMS) decoder compared to the layered binary sum-product decoder over both depolarizing and Markovian channels. Using the QBLNMS decoder over a quaternary alphabet, we demonstrate that correlated Pauli errors can be effectively handled within the decoding framework. Furthermore, under the QBLNMS decoding, the proposed codes achieve [MATH] performance improvements compared to prior works and can effectively handle both random and burst errors. The code constructions are scalable across various coding rates and quantum payloads, crucial for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

.
tldr: Construction of entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC codes with improved error correction performance.
motivation: To develop efficient quantum error correction codes for practical quantum communication and computing.
method: They construct families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes using structured tilings of permutation matrices, and propose an encoding scheme and a quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum decoder.
result: The codes achieve nearly one order improvement in error-correction performance compared to existing methods, and are scalable across coding rates and payloads.
conclusion: The proposed codes are resource-efficient and can effectively handle random and burst errors, making them suitable for practical quantum systems.

title: Stabilizer Ranks, Barnes Wall Lattices And Magic Monotones
authors: Amolak Ratan Kalra And Pulkit Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2179 (2026).

In 2024, Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck showed a connection between the Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states and Clifford operations. In this work, we study their results and relate them to the problem of lower bounding stabilizer ranks. We show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which reproduces the linear-by-log lower bound for [MATH], i.e, on the approximate stabilizer rank of [MATH]. In fact, we show that the lower bound holds even when the fidelity between the approximation and [MATH] is exponentially small, which is currently the best lower bound in this regime. Next, we define a new magic monotone for pure states, the Barnes Wall norm, and its corresponding approximate variant. We upper bound these monotones by the [MATH]-count of state preparation, and also by the stabilizer ranks. In particular, the upper bound given by the [MATH]-count is tight, in the sense that we exhibit states that achieve the bound. Apart from these results, we give a Fidelity Amplification algorithm, which provides a trade-off between approximation error and the stabilizer rank. As a corollary, it gives us a way to compose approximate stabilizer decompositions into approximate decompositions of their tensor products. Finally, we provide an alternate, elementary proof of the existence and density of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks, which was first proven by Lovitz and Steffan (2022), where they used results from algebraic geometry.

.
tldr: The paper connects Barnes Wall lattices to stabilizer ranks and defines a new magic monotone, providing bounds and algorithms for quantum resource theories.
motivation: To advance the understanding of stabilizer ranks and magic monotones, which are crucial for quantifying non-Clifford resources in quantum computation and error correction.
method: The authors use algebraic and lattice theory, particularly Barnes Wall lattices, to derive lower bounds on stabilizer fidelity, define a new magic monotone called the Barnes Wall norm, and present a fidelity amplification algorithm.
result: They prove the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, show it holds for exponentially small fidelity, provide tight upper bounds on the new monotone via T-count, and demonstrate a trade-off between approximation error and stabilizer rank.
conclusion: The work provides new tools and results for stabilizer rank theory and magic monotones, advancing the field of quantum resource theories and potentially improving magic state distillation protocols.

title: Contextuality Under Characterized Loss: Quantifying Missing Contextual Information Via Channel-transported Relative Entropy
authors: Ofer Harel And Kun Chen Arash Esmaili Zaghi
abstract: Relative-entropy measures of contextuality quantify the statistical distance between an empirical model and the noncontextual set. We study how this established quantity changes when an experiment is observed through a characterized loss mechanism. Each attempted trial is retained in the analysis, with missed outcomes represented by context-labeled no-click symbols, and the same stochastic observation channel is applied to the target model and every noncontextual comparator. Under this common-channel transportability assumption, the data-processing inequality gives an observed-data contextual divergence that cannot exceed its complete-data value. We define the absolute contextual-information loss and its normalized ratio, the fraction of missing contextual information (FMCI). We prove general reference-set contraction, exact scaling under missing completely at random loss, a cellwise erasure sandwich, a no-exact-hiding result under strictly positive retention, and additive and multiplicative decompositions for sequential design and detector channels. We also separate response dependence from disturbance of shared marginals and clarify why outcomes of unchosen incompatible contexts are not model-neutral missing entries. The theory is evaluated on the perfect-anticorrelation three-cycle, the Klyachko–Can–Binicioğlu–Shumovsky pentagon, and the Peres–Mermin magic square. The hidden-variable and inequality-constrained optimizations agree to within nats. Exhaustive enumeration of all context subcovers shows that, for these three canonical benchmark points, every proper subcover is noncontextual. A scan of a tunable outcome-dependent loss family confirms that exact population hiding occurs only on the zero-retention boundary, while finite-sample detectability can deteriorate well before that boundary. For a known finite-alphabet erasure channel with cellwise retention probabilities we give an exact identification criterion, regular asymptotic and Fieller inference for FMCI, and diagnostics that withhold scalar ratio inference near the noncontextual boundary. Unknown outcome-dependent loss is handled by a calibration-constrained sensitivity workflow and union confidence sets. FMCI is therefore a conditional diagnostic of information attenuation under a declared observation channel, not a replacement for loophole-free contextuality certification.
tldr: This paper defines a measure of contextual information loss under a characterized observation channel, using relative entropy between empirical models and the noncontextual set.
motivation: Contextuality is a non-classical resource, but experiments suffer losses that obscure it; the paper aims to quantify how much contextual information is lost under such conditions.
method: The authors consider a common stochastic observation channel applied to both target and comparator models, use the data-processing inequality to show that observed-data divergence is lower-bounded, and define the fraction of missing contextual information (FMCI) with proofs of contraction and scaling properties.
result: They derive exact conditions for retention, show exact hiding only at zero retention, and provide asymptotic inference and calibration workflows for the loss parameters.
conclusion: FMCI is a conditional diagnostic of information attenuation under a declared observation channel, not a replacement for loophole-free contextuality certification.

title: Modulator-Assisted Zeno Control Of Energy Transfer In Quantum Batteries
authors: Songbo Xie, Manas Sajjan, Ashok Ajoy, And Sabre Kais
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2178 (2026).

Efficient operation of quantum batteries requires not only fast energy transfer but also the ability to halt the charging process to prevent reverse flow. Existing approaches typically rely on direct control of the charger-battery interaction, which can be experimentally demanding. Here we propose a modulator-assisted quantum battery protocol that enables indirect control of energy transfer while keeping the interaction always on. By applying repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit, we exploit a Zeno-like mechanism to dynamically reshape the effective Hamiltonian and switch the charger-battery coupling on and off. We demonstrate this mechanism in a minimal three-body model and show that it remains effective beyond the ideal fast-control limit. We further extend the protocol to a collective many-body architecture, where it preserves the characteristic enhancement of charging power, scaling as [MATH] with the number of battery units. We also discuss a possible implementation in an NV-[MATH]C spin platform. Our results establish modulator-assisted Zeno control as a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries.

.
tldr: Proposes a modulator-assisted Zeno control protocol for quantum batteries to switch charging on/off while keeping the interaction always on.
motivation: Efficient quantum battery operation requires halting charging to prevent reverse flow, but existing approaches rely on demanding direct control of the charger-battery interaction.
method: Apply repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit, exploiting a Zeno-like mechanism to dynamically reshape the effective Hamiltonian and toggle the charger-battery coupling.
result: Demonstrates the mechanism in a minimal three-body model and shows it remains effective beyond the fast-control limit, extending to a collective many-body architecture with enhanced charging power scaling.
conclusion: Establishes modulator-assisted Zeno control as a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries.

title: Quantifiers And Witnesses For The Nonclassicality Of Measurements And Of States
authors: Yujie Zhang, Yìlè Yīng, And David Schmid
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2180 (2026).

In recent work [Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050], we proposed a unified notion of nonclassicality that applies to arbitrary processes in quantum theory, including individual quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof. This notion is derived from the principle of generalized noncontextuality, but in a novel manner that applies to individual processes rather than full experiments or theories. In the present work, we develop semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of states, sources, measurements, and sets thereof. These theory-dependent methods complement theory-independent approaches based on noncontextuality inequalities. We demonstrate the framework through a variety of explicit examples.

.
tldr: This paper develops semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of quantum states, sources, and measurements, based on generalized noncontextuality.
motivation: To provide practical, theory-dependent tools for detecting nonclassicality that complement theory-independent noncontextuality inequalities, which are often difficult to apply.
method: They construct SDP-based certificates and witnesses that characterize nonclassicality of individual processes, and demonstrate the framework with explicit examples.
result: The framework is shown to be effective across various examples, offering a new approach to quantify and witness nonclassicality.
conclusion: This work provides a valuable complement to existing noncontextuality tests, enabling efficient detection of nonclassicality in practical scenarios.

title: Quantum Phase Estimation With Optimal Confidence Interval Using Three Control Qubits
authors: Kaur Kristjuhan And Dominic W. Berry
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2193 (2026).

Quantum phase estimation is an important routine in many quantum algorithms, particularly for estimating the ground state energy in quantum chemistry simulations. This estimation involves applying powers of a unitary to the ground state, controlled by an auxiliary state prepared on a control register. In many applications the goal is to provide a confidence interval for the phase estimate, and optimal performance is provided by a discrete prolate spheroidal sequence. We show how to prepare the corresponding state in a far more efficient way than prior work. We find that a matrix product state representation with a bond dimension of 4 is sufficient to give a highly accurate approximation for all dimensions tested, up to [MATH]. This matrix product state can be efficiently prepared using a sequence of simple three-qubit operations. When the dimension is a power of 2, the phase estimation can be performed with only three qubits for the control register, making it suitable for early-generation fault-tolerant quantum computers with a limited number of logical qubits.

﻿

.
tldr: This paper presents an efficient method to prepare the optimal control state for quantum phase estimation using matrix product states, requiring only three qubits when the dimension is a power of two.
motivation: Quantum phase estimation is crucial for many quantum algorithms, and the optimal confidence interval requires a specific control state; preparing this state efficiently is important for early fault-tolerant quantum computers.
method: The authors use matrix product state (MPS) representation with bond dimension 4 to approximate the desired state, and show it can be prepared with simple three-qubit operations; they also show that when dimension is a power of 2, only three control qubits are needed.
result: They find that bond dimension 4 suffices for accurate approximation across all tested dimensions, and the state preparation is highly efficient, suitable for early fault-tolerant devices.
conclusion: This work significantly reduces the resources needed for optimal quantum phase estimation, making it more practical for near-term quantum computers.

title: Efficient Graph State Generation In Linear Optics
authors: Seungbeom Chin And William John Munro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2189 (2026).

Graph states are central resources for quantum information processing, supporting applications in computation, communication, and error correction. In photonic systems, they are typically assembled from smaller entangled states using probabilistic fusion gates, which demand many photons and suffer from low success rates. We present an optimized scheme for directly generating caterpillar graph states (CGSs)—essential resource states for constructing high-dimensional lattice graph states—using only single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements. Based on the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture, our method produces CGSs efficiently. For CGSs of length [MATH], it requires [MATH] fewer photons and achieves a success rate [MATH] times higher than fusion-based approaches. These results demonstrate that the LQG picture provides a powerful and flexible route to generating complex photonic graph states for efficient quantum information processing.

.
tldr: This paper presents an optimized scheme for generating caterpillar graph states using single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements, achieving higher efficiency than fusion-based approaches.
motivation: Graph states are essential for quantum information processing, but current generation methods using probabilistic fusion gates are photon-intensive and have low success rates.
method: The proposed method uses the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture and employs only single-photon sources, linear optical elements, and heralded measurements to directly generate caterpillar graph states.
result: For caterpillar graph states of a given length, the scheme requires fewer photons and achieves a success rate multiple times higher than fusion-based approaches.
conclusion: The LQG picture provides a powerful and flexible route to generating complex photonic graph states, enabling more efficient quantum information processing.

title: Atommovr: An Open-source Simulation Framework For Rearrangement In Atomic Arrays
authors: Nikhil K Harle, Bo-Yu Chen, Bob Bao, And Hannes Bernien
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2177 (2026).

The task of atom rearrangement has emerged in the last decade as a fundamental building block in the development of neutral atom-based quantum processors. As such processors grow to thousands of atoms, it becomes increasingly important to design algorithms robust to experimental sources of error. While recent progress has been made towards developing algorithms with favorable time scaling, such work has been limited to noiseless settings. Moreover, there is a lack of open-source code for reproducing and benchmarking existing algorithms. To address these deficiencies, we develop an open-source simulation framework, atommovr, and leverage it to study three distinct settings: 1) time-optimal, noiseless rearrangement, 2) noisy rearrangement under realistic error models, and 3) noiseless dual-species rearrangement. We extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, study advantageous strategies across different error regimes, and develop a novel dual-species algorithm, InsideOut, capable of avoiding 'blocked' configurations with a near-unity success rate. We hope that atommovr can serve as a common tool for the community to study rearrangement, lower the barrier to entry for new experimental groups, and stimulate progress in developing algorithms tailored to minimize atom loss in experiment.

.
tldr: This paper introduces atommovr, an open-source simulation framework for atom rearrangement in neutral atom arrays, and proposes a new dual-species algorithm (InsideOut) that avoids blocked configurations.
motivation: As neutral-atom quantum processors scale up, reliable atom rearrangement becomes essential, but existing algorithms are not robust to noise and there is a lack of open-source benchmarking tools.
method: The authors develop a modular simulation framework (atommovr) and study time-optimal, noisy, and dual-species rearrangement settings, introducing the InsideOut algorithm for dual-species cases.
result: They extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, compare strategies across error regimes, and demonstrate near-unity success rate for dual-species rearrangement with InsideOut.
conclusion: The framework provides a community resource for benchmarking and developing rearrangement algorithms, advancing neutral atom quantum computing.

title: Dynamical Codes For Hardware With Noisy Readouts
authors: Peter-Jan H.S. Derks, Alex Townsend-Teague, Jens Eisert, Markus S. Kesselring, Oscar Higgott, And Benjamin J. Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2176 (2026).

Dynamical stabilizer codes may offer a practical route to large-scale quantum computation. Such codes are defined by a schedule of error-detecting measurements, which allows for flexibility in their construction. In this work, we ask how best to optimise the measurement schedule of dynamically condensed colour codes in various limits of noise bias. We take a particular focus on the setting where measurements introduce more noise than unitary and idling operations – a noise model relevant to some hardware proposals. For measurement-biased noise models, we improve code performance by strategically repeating measurements within the schedule. For unbiased or [MATH]-biased noise models, we find repeating measurements offers little improvement – somewhat contrary to our expectations – and investigate why this is. To perform this analysis, we generalise a metric called the teraquop footprint to the teraquop volume. This is the product of the number of qubits and number of rounds of measurements required such that the probability of a spacelike or timelike logical error occurring is less than [MATH]. In most cases, we find differences in performance are primarily due to the number of rounds of measurements required, rather than the number of qubits – emphasising the importance of using the teraquop volume in the analysis. Additionally, our results provide another example of the importance of making use of correlated errors when decoding, in that using belief matching rather than minimum-weight perfect matching can turn a worst-performing code under a given noise model into a best-performing code.

.
tldr: This paper optimizes measurement schedules for dynamical color codes under measurement-biased noise, introducing a teraquop volume metric and showing that repeating measurements helps in some regimes and that belief matching decoding improves performance.
motivation: Quantum error correction with noisy readouts requires optimizing measurement schedules; existing metrics may not capture trade-offs between qubit count and measurement rounds.
method: They generalize the teraquop footprint to teraquop volume and analyze dynamical color codes under various noise biases, comparing measurement repetition strategies and decoding algorithms.
result: Repeating measurements improves performance for measurement-biased noise but not for unbiased or X-biased noise; performance differences are mainly due to measurement rounds, and belief matching outperforms minimum-weight perfect matching.
conclusion: The teraquop volume metric is important for evaluating dynamical codes, and using correlated error decoding can significantly improve performance.

title: Non-commutative Optimization Problems With Differential Constraints
authors: Mateus Araújo, Andrew J. P. Garner, And Miguel Navascues
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2169 (2026).

Non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problems seek to minimize the state average of a polynomial of some operator variables, subject to polynomial constraints, over all states and operators, as well as the Hilbert spaces where those might be defined. Many of these problems are known to admit a complete hierarchy of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. In this work, we consider a variant of NPO problems where a subset of the operator variables satisfies a system of ordinary differential equations. We prove that, under mild conditions of operator boundedness, for every such problem one can construct a standard NPO problem with the same solution. This allows us to define a complete hierarchy of SDPs to tackle the original differential problem. We apply this method to bound averages of local observables in quantum spin systems subject to a Hamiltonian evolution (i.e., a quench). We find that, even in the thermodynamic limit of infinitely many sites, low levels of the hierarchy provide very good approximations for reasonably long evolution times.

.
tldr: This paper extends non-commutative polynomial optimization to problems with differential constraints, enabling a complete SDP hierarchy for bounding observables in quantum quenches.
motivation: To tackle time-dependent quantum optimization problems, such as those arising in non-equilibrium spin systems, and to provide a computational tool for bounding physical quantities.
method: The authors prove that any non-commutative optimization problem with differential constraints can be rewritten as a standard NPO problem under boundedness conditions, then apply the existing NPO SDP hierarchy to the quench dynamics of quantum spin systems.
result: Low levels of the hierarchy yield accurate bounds on local observables for reasonably long evolution times, even in the thermodynamic limit.
conclusion: The proposed method offers a general, rigorous framework for solving a class of time-dependent quantum optimization problems, with promising applications in quantum thermodynamics and many-body physics.

title: Quantum Resource Comparison For Two Leading Surface Code Lattice Surgery Approaches
authors: Tyler Leblond And Ryan S. Bennink
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2187 (2026).

Hamiltonian simulation is one of the most promising candidates for the demonstration of quantum advantage within the next ten years, and several studies have proposed end-to-end resource estimates for executing such algorithms on fault-tolerant quantum processors. Usually, these resource estimates are based upon the assumption that quantum error correction is implemented using the surface code, and that the best surface code compilation scheme involves serializing input circuits by eliminating all Clifford gates. This transformation is thought to make best use of the native multi-body measurement (lattice surgery) instruction set available to surface codes. Some work, however, has suggested that direct compilation from Clifford+T to lattice surgery operations may be beneficial for circuits that have high degrees of logical parallelism. In this study, we analyze the resource costs for implementing Hamiltonian simulation using example approaches from each of these leading surface code compilation families. The Hamiltonians whose dynamics we consider are those of the transverse-field Ising model in several geometries, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and the [MATH] complex under a time-varying magnetic field. We show, among other things, that the optimal scheme depends on whether Hamiltonian simulation is implemented using the quantum signal processing or Trotter-Suzuki algorithms, with Trotterization benefiting by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation for these applications. Our results suggest that surface code quantum computers should not have a one-size-fits-all compilation scheme, but that smart compilers should predict the optimal scheme based upon high-level quantities from logical circuits such as average circuit density, numbers of logical qubits, and T fraction.

.
tldr: This paper compares two surface code compilation schemes for Hamiltonian simulation, finding that the optimal approach depends on the simulation algorithm, with Trotterization significantly benefiting from direct Clifford+T compilation.
motivation: To determine which surface code compilation strategy is more resource-efficient for Hamiltonian simulation on fault-tolerant quantum computers, as previous work suggested that serializing circuits to eliminate Clifford gates might not always be optimal.
method: The authors analyze resource costs for implementing Hamiltonian simulation using two compilation families: one that serializes input circuits by eliminating all Clifford gates, and another that directly compiles Clifford+T to lattice surgery operations. They consider multiple Hamiltonians and both quantum signal processing and Trotter-Suzuki algorithms.
result: They show that the optimal scheme varies with the simulation algorithm; Trotterization benefits by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation, while quantum signal processing may benefit from the other approach, indicating no one-size-fits-all compilation.
conclusion: Surface code quantum computers should employ smart compilers that predict the optimal compilation scheme based on logical circuit characteristics like density, qubit count, and T fraction.

title: Disorder-Induced Entanglement Phase Transitions In Non-Hermitian Systems With Skin Effects
authors: Kai Li, Ze-Chuan Liu, And Yong Xu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2186 (2026).

Non-Hermitian dynamics is ubiquitous in various physical systems. While recent study shows that such a dynamics leads to an area-law scaling of the entanglement entropy due to the non-Hermitian skin effects, it remains unclear how disorder changes the behavior of the entanglement entropy in a non-Hermitian system with skin effects. Here we study the dynamics of a many-body state of free fermions in the paradigmatic Hatano-Nelson model with open boundaries, and find that the area-law behavior of the entanglement entropy in the pristine Hatano-Nelson model develops into a logarithmic scaling for small disorder strength. As we further increase the disorder strength, the system reenters an area-law regime through an entanglement phase transition. At the critical point, the entanglement entropy exhibits a universal algebraic scaling. We further demonstrate the absence of a conformal invariance in the log-law regime by examining the subsystem entanglement entropy, the connected correlation function and the mutual information. Finally, we show the existence of disorder induced entanglement phase transitions in the Hatano-Nelson model with periodic boundaries.

.
tldr: This paper investigates how disorder changes entanglement entropy scaling in non-Hermitian systems with skin effects, revealing transitions between area-law and logarithmic scaling.
motivation: Previous work showed non-Hermitian skin effects lead to area-law entanglement, but the impact of disorder on this behavior was unknown.
method: They studied the dynamics of free fermions in the Hatano-Nelson model with open and periodic boundaries, computing entanglement entropy, connected correlation functions, and mutual information for various disorder strengths.
result: They found that small disorder induces a logarithmic scaling, which transitions back to area-law at stronger disorder, with algebraic scaling at the critical point and no conformal invariance in the log-law regime.
conclusion: The results demonstrate disorder-induced entanglement phase transitions in non-Hermitian systems, offering insights into the interplay of disorder and non-Hermitian dynamics.

title: Promise Of Graph Sparsification And Decomposition For Noise Reduction In Qaoa: Analysis For Trapped-Ion Compilations
authors: Jai Moondra, Phillip C. Lotshaw, Greg Mohler, And Swati Gupta
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2185 (2026).

We develop new approximate compilation schemes that significantly reduce the expense of compiling the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for solving the Max-Cut problem. Our main focus is on compilation with trapped-ion simulators using Pauli-[MATH] operations and all-to-all Ising Hamiltonian [MATH] evolution generated by Molmer-Sorensen or optical dipole force interactions, though some of our results also apply to standard gate-based compilations. Our results are based on principles of graph sparsification and decomposition; the former reduces the number of edges in a graph while maintaining its cut structure, while the latter breaks a weighted graph into a small number of unweighted graphs. Though these techniques have been used as heuristics in various hybrid quantum algorithms, there have been no guarantees on their performance, to the best of our knowledge. This work provides the first provable guarantees using sparsification and decomposition to improve quantum noise resilience and reduce quantum circuit complexity. For quantum hardware that uses edge-by-edge QAOA compilations, sparsification leads to a direct reduction in circuit complexity. For trapped-ion quantum simulators implementing all-to-all [MATH] pulses, we show that for a [MATH] factor loss in the Max-Cut approximation ([MATH], our compilations improve the (worst-case) number of [MATH] pulses from [MATH] to [MATH] and the (worst-case) number of Pauli-[MATH] bit flips from [MATH] to [MATH] for [MATH]-node graphs. This is an asymptotic improvement for any constant [MATH]. We demonstrate that significant improvements to the approximation ratio are obtained using decomposition in simulated trapped-ion experiments with dephasing noise. We further present a generic argument showing that sparsification results in an exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bound in digital computing schemes based on one- and two-qubit gates, which are relevant to a wide variety of hardwares such as superconducting qubits and certain neutral atom or trapped ion setups, and more sophisticated noise models. We anticipate these approximate compilation techniques will be useful tools in a variety of future quantum computing experiments.

.
tldr: 提出基于图稀疏化和分解的QAOA近似编译方案，显著减少trapped-ion模拟器的电路复杂度并提升噪声韧性，并提供首个可证明的改进保证。
motivation: QAOA编译通常需要大量操作，导致噪声累积；稀疏化和分解虽被用作启发式，但缺乏理论保证，本文旨在提供严谨的改进。
method: 利用图稀疏化减少边数（保持割结构），以及图分解将加权图拆为少量未加权图，针对trapped-ion编译中的Pauli-X和全对Ising脉冲进行优化。
result: 对于Max-Cut，在近似比损失ε下，最坏情况脉冲数从O(n^2)降至O(n log n)，Pauli-X翻转次数从O(n^2)降至O(n log n)，并在模拟dephasing噪声实验中验证了近似比改进。
conclusion: 这些近似编译技术提供可证明的电路复杂度和噪声韧性改善，可广泛应用于各类量子计算硬件，提升实验可行性。

title: Generalised All-optical Cat Correction
authors: Olivier Landon-Cardinal And Nicolás Quesada Ari John Boon
abstract: We have generalised an all-optical telecorrection protocol for the higher orders of the cat code, and show that with these higher orders we can achieve target performance at substantially reduced iteration counts at the cost of a higher mean photon-number. We also introduce a probabilistic scheme for correcting deformation of the state, which highlights two interesting abilities of telecorrection: to encode new sets of transformations, and to change the basis of the code. We find that for a target channel fidelity of over a channel with of loss, a third-order cat code requires times fewer telecorrection iterations than a first-order one, at a cost of a -fold increase in mean photon-number.
tldr: This paper generalizes an all-optical telecorrection protocol for higher-order cat codes, showing reduced iteration counts at the cost of higher mean photon-number, and introduces a probabilistic scheme for correcting state deformation.
motivation: To improve the efficiency of quantum error correction for cat codes, which are crucial for optical quantum computing, by exploring higher-order codes and new correction strategies.
method: The authors generalize the telecorrection protocol to higher-order cat codes and introduce a probabilistic scheme for handling state deformation, analyzing the trade-off between iteration count and mean photon-number.
result: For a target channel fidelity under loss, a third-order cat code requires fewer telecorrection iterations than a first-order one, but with increased mean photon-number; the probabilistic scheme also enables new transformations and basis changes.
conclusion: Higher-order cat codes offer a favorable trade-off for telecorrection, and the probabilistic scheme expands the capabilities of all-optical error correction.

title: Hoare Meets Heisenberg: A Lightweight Logic For Quantum Programs
authors: Aarthi Sundaram, Robert Rand, Kartik Singhal, Youngchan Cho, And Brad Lackey
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2172 (2026).

We show that Gottesman's (1998) semantics for Clifford circuits based on the Heisenberg representation gives rise to a lightweight Hoare-like logic for efficiently characterizing a common subset of quantum programs. Our applications include (i) certifying whether auxiliary qubits can be safely disposed of, (ii) determining if a system is separable across a given bipartition, (iii) checking the transversality of a gate with respect to a given stabilizer code, and (iv) computing post-measurement states for computational basis measurements. Further, this logic is extended to accommodate universal quantum computing by deriving Hoare triples for the [MATH]-gate, multiply-controlled unitaries such as the Toffoli gate, and some gate injection circuits that use associated magic states. A number of interesting results emerge from this logic, including a lower bound on the number of [MATH] gates necessary to perform a multiply-controlled [MATH] gate.

.
tldr: A lightweight Hoare logic for quantum programs based on the Heisenberg representation enables efficient reasoning about Clifford circuits and extends to universal quantum computing.
motivation: To provide a simple and efficient method for verifying properties of quantum programs, such as disposability of auxiliary qubits, separability, transversality, and post-measurement states.
method: Uses Gottesman's Heisenberg representation to derive Hoare triples for Clifford circuits, and extends to universal quantum computing via derived triples for T-gates, Toffoli, and magic state injection.
result: Introduces a logic that can certify these properties and also yields a lower bound on the number of T-gates for multiply-controlled gates.
conclusion: The logic is a lightweight and powerful tool for reasoning about quantum programs, with potential applications in quantum error correction and quantum compilation.

title: Construction Of Local Unitary Equivalent Quantum States Via Local Unitary Equivalent Orthogonal Arrays
authors: Xiao Zhang, Shanqi Pang, Mengqian Chen And Shao-Ming Fei
abstract: Two orthogonal arrays (OAs) are local unitary (LU) equivalent if they lead to LU-equivalent quantum states. Finding LU-equivalent OAs is an open problem posed by Goyeneche et al (Phys. Rev. A90 022316). In this paper, we develop methods of constructing infinite families of LU-equivalent OAs, both fixed-level and mixed-level, by investigating the constructions, structures and properties of OAs. We consequently provide a solution to the open problem. The results significantly advance our understanding of LU-equivalent quantum states and their potential applications in quantum information processing.
tldr: This paper constructs infinite families of local unitary equivalent quantum states via local unitary equivalent orthogonal arrays, solving an open problem in quantum information.
motivation: The open problem of finding LU-equivalent orthogonal arrays is addressed, as such arrays lead to LU-equivalent quantum states, which are important for quantum information processing.
method: The authors develop methods for constructing infinite families of LU-equivalent OAs, both fixed-level and mixed-level, by investigating their constructions, structures, and properties.
result: They provide a solution to the open problem and obtain infinite families of LU-equivalent quantum states.
conclusion: The results advance understanding of LU-equivalent quantum states and their potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Fourier Analysis Of Many-body Transition Amplitudes And States
authors: Gabriel Dufour And Andreas Buchleitner
abstract: Particle-exchange symmetry shapes the counting statistics of many-body systems by giving rise to multiple alternative evolutions whose transition amplitudes interfere. Here, we apply a Fourier transform over the symmetric group to the collection of many-body transition amplitudes connecting two states of an -particle system. This provides a decomposition of the counting statistics of many-body interference experiments into contributions associated with distinct irreducible exchange symmetries. As a first application of our formalism, we consider bosons or fermions which are rendered partially distinguishable from one another through unobserved degrees of freedom, and whose state is also subjected to a Fourier analysis. We thereby obtain a systematic description of partial distinguishability, which is both an important experimental noise source and a possible handle for the control of many-body interference. As a second application, we identify mechanisms responsible for completely destructive interference in many-body systems with other exchange symmetries than those of bosons or fermions. For an interferometer implementing the discrete Fourier transform unitary, we predict many instances of such suppressed transitions.
tldr: Applies Fourier transform over the symmetric group to many-body transition amplitudes, decomposing counting statistics into exchange-symmetry contributions and providing a systematic description of partial distinguishability.
motivation: Particle-exchange symmetry gives rise to interfering multiple evolutions in many-body systems; partially distinguishable particles are both a noise source and a control handle for many-body interference.
method: A Fourier transform over the symmetric group is applied to the collection of many-body transition amplitudes, yielding a decomposition into contributions from distinct irreducible exchange symmetries. The states are also Fourier-analyzed to handle partial distinguishability.

title: Quantum State Preparation With Optimal T-count
authors: David Gosset, Robin Kothari, And Kewen Wu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2168 (2026).

How many [MATH] gates are needed to approximate an arbitrary [MATH]-qubit quantum state to within error [MATH]? Improving prior work of Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, we show that the optimal asymptotic scaling is [MATH] if we allow ancilla qubits. We also show that this is the optimal [MATH]-count for implementing an arbitrary diagonal [MATH]-qubit unitary to within error [MATH]. We describe applications in which a tensor product of many single-qubit unitaries can be synthesized in parallel for the price of one.

.
tldr: This paper determines the optimal asymptotic T-count for preparing arbitrary n-qubit quantum states and implementing diagonal unitaries with ancilla qubits.
motivation: Understanding the minimal number of T gates needed for quantum state preparation is fundamental for optimizing quantum circuits, especially in fault-tolerant quantum computing where T gates are costly.
method: The authors build on prior work by Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, providing improved upper bounds and proving optimality using techniques from quantum circuit synthesis and approximation theory.
result: They show the optimal T-count scales as Θ(4^n) for arbitrary n-qubit states and diagonal unitaries, and also demonstrate applications where parallel synthesis of many single-qubit unitaries can be done for the price of one.
conclusion: The work establishes tight bounds for T-count in state preparation and unitary synthesis, which is a key step toward resource-efficient quantum compilation.

title: Non-Gaussian Noise Magnetometry Using Local Spin Qubits
authors: Jonathan B. Curtis, Amir Yacoby, And Eugene Demler
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2197 (2026).

Atomic scale qubits, as may be realized in nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, offer the opportunity to study magnetic field noise with nanometer scale spatial resolution. Using these spin qubits, one can learn a great deal about the magnetic-field noise correlations, and correspondingly the collective-mode spectra, in quantum materials and devices. However, to date these tools have been essentially restricted to studying Gaussian noise processes – equivalent to linear-response. In this work we will show how to extend these techniques beyond the Gaussian regime and show how to unambiguously measure higher-order magnetic noise cumulants in a local, spatially resolved way. We unveil two protocols for doing this; the first uses a single spin-qubit and different dynamical decoupling sequences to extract non-Markovian and non-Gaussian spin-echo noise. The second protocol uses two-qubit coincidence measurements to study spatially non-local cumulants in the magnetic noise. We then demonstrate the utility of these protocols by considering a model of a bath of non-interacting two-level systems, as well as a model involving spatially correlated magnetic fluctuations near a second-order Ising phase transition. In both cases, we highlight how this technique can be used to measure in a real many-body system how fluctuation dynamics converge towards the central limit theorem as a function of effective bath size. We then conclude by discussing some promising applications and extensions of this method.

.
tldr: This paper introduces protocols for measuring higher-order, non-Gaussian magnetic noise using spin qubits such as NV centers, extending noise characterization beyond Gaussian approximations.
motivation: Existing spin qubit-based noise magnetometry only captures Gaussian noise (linear response), limiting study of collective-mode spectra. The authors aim to measure non-Gaussian noise cumulants in a local, spatially resolved manner.
method: Two protocols are proposed: one using a single spin qubit with dynamical decoupling sequences to extract non-Markovian non-Gaussian spin-echo noise, and another using two-qubit coincidence measurements for spatially non-local cumulants. Models of non-interacting two-level systems and a second-order Ising phase transition are analyzed.
result: The protocols enable measurement of higher-order magnetic noise cumulants, demonstrating convergence towards the central limit theorem as effective bath size increases in many-body systems.
conclusion: The method can probe non-Gaussian noise in real quantum materials and devices, offering new insights into fluctuation dynamics and potential applications in quantum sensing and material characterization.

title: On The Relation Between Perspective-neutral, Algebraic, And Effective Quantum Reference Frames
authors: Julian de Vuyst, Philipp A. Hoehn, And Artur Tsobanjan
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2196 (2026).

The framework of internal quantum reference frames (QRFs) constitutes a universal toolset for dealing with symmetries in quantum theory and has led to new revelations in quantum gravity, gauge theories and foundational physics. Multiple approaches have emerged, sometimes differing in scope and the way symmetries are implemented, raising the question as to their relation. Here, we investigate the relation between three approaches to QRFs for gauge symmetries, namely the [MATH] semiclassical, [MATH], and [MATH] (PN) approaches. Rather than constructing Hilbert spaces, as the PN approach, the effective approach is based on a quantum phase space parametrized by expectation values and fluctuations, while the emphasis of the algebraic approach is on the state space of complex linear functionals on a kinematical algebra. Nevertheless, external frame information is treated as gauge in all three formalisms, manifested in constraints on states and algebra. We show that these three approaches are, in fact, equivalent for ideal QRFs, distinguished by sharp orientations, which is the previous setting of the first two approaches. Our demonstration pertains to single constraints, including relativistic ones, and encompasses QRF changes. In particular, the QRF transformations of the PN framework agree semiclassically with those of the older effective approach, by which it was inspired. As a physical application, we explore the QRF covariance of uncertainties and fluctuations, which turn out to be frame dependent. This is particularly well-suited for the effective and algebraic approaches, for which these quantities form a natural basis. Finally, we pave the way towards extending these two approaches to non-ideal QRFs by studying the projection and gauge-fixing operations of the Page-Wootters formalism, built into the PN framework, on algebraic states.

.
tldr: This paper compares three formalisms for quantum reference frames under gauge symmetries and shows they are equivalent for ideal frames, with frame-dependent uncertainties.
motivation: To understand and unify different approaches to quantum reference frames, which are relevant to quantum gravity and gauge theories.
method: The authors analyze the semiclassical, algebraic, and perspective-neutral approaches, demonstrating their equivalence for ideal QRFs with sharp orientations, and study projection and gauge-fixing operations for non-ideal cases.
