result: The three approaches are shown to be equivalent for ideal QRFs, and quantum reference frame transformations agree semiclassically, with uncertainties and fluctuations being frame-dependent.
conclusion: The work paves the way for extending these approaches to non-ideal QRFs and provides a unified understanding of quantum reference frames.

title: Unconditional Quantum Advantage For Sampling With Shallow Circuits
authors: Adam Bene Watts And Natalie Parham
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2188 (2026).

Recent work by Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig showed that there exists a search problem that a constant-depth quantum circuit can solve, but that any constant-depth classical circuit with bounded fan-in cannot. They also pose the question: Can we achieve a similar proof of separation for an input-independent sampling task? In this paper, we show that the answer to this question is yes when the number of random input bits given to the classical circuit is bounded. We introduce a distribution [MATH] over [MATH] and construct a constant-depth uniform quantum circuit family [MATH] such that [MATH] samples from a distribution close to [MATH] in total variation distance. For any [MATH] we also prove, unconditionally, that any classical circuit with bounded fan-in gates that takes as input [MATH] i.i.d. Bernouli random variables with entropy [MATH] and produces output close to [MATH] in total variation distance has depth [MATH]. This gives an unconditional proof that constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from distributions that can't be reproduced by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits, even up to additive error. We also show a similar separation between constant-depth quantum circuits with advice and classical circuits with bounded fan-in and fan-out, but access to an unbounded number of i.i.d random inputs. The distribution [MATH] and classical circuit lower bounds are inspired by work of Viola, in which he shows a different (but related) distribution cannot be sampled from approximately by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits.

.
tldr: This paper proves an unconditional separation between constant-depth quantum circuits and bounded-fan-in classical circuits for sampling tasks.
motivation: Following Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig's separation for search problems, the authors ask whether a similar separation holds for sampling tasks without input dependence, aiming to extend quantum advantage results.
method: They introduce a specific distribution and construct a constant-depth quantum circuit sampling from it, then prove lower bounds on the depth of any classical circuit with bounded fan-in gates that approximates this distribution to within additive error.
result: They show that any classical bounded-fan-in circuit requiring a bounded amount of input randomness (with entropy r) must have depth at least Ω(log r) to sample from the distribution, while a constant-depth quantum circuit suffices, unconditionally.
conclusion: This provides an unconditional proof that constant-depth quantum circuits outperform constant-depth classical circuits in sampling tasks, contributing to quantum computational advantage.

title: Pilot-Wave Simulator: Exact Classical Sampling From Ideal And Noisy Quantum Circuits Up To Hundreds Of Qubits
authors: Gleb Kalachev, Pavel Mosharev, Zuoheng Zou, Pavel Panteleev, And Man-Hong Yung
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2173 (2026).

Quantum circuit simulators running on classical computers offer a vital platform for designing, testing, and optimizing quantum algorithms, driving innovation despite limited access to real quantum hardware. However, their scalability is inherently constrained by exponential memory and computational overhead, which restricts accurate simulation of large-scale quantum circuits and often results in approximate output distributions. Here, we propose an exact sampling algorithm that integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, wherein a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. As a demonstration, we target the challenge of generating samples from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating both depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models. These results enable further validation of several assumptions and conjectures at a scale previously out of reach, significantly expanding the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research.

.
tldr: This paper introduces an exact classical sampling algorithm for quantum circuits using tensor network contraction and a Markov process, demonstrated on QAOA circuits up to 476 qubits.
motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is limited by exponential overhead, hindering validation of large-scale quantum algorithms. The authors aim to overcome this with an exact sampling method.
method: The algorithm integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, where a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit.
result: The method is applied to ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models, enabling sampling from these circuits.
conclusion: This work significantly expands the scale at which quantum circuits can be classically simulated, aiding in the validation of quantum algorithm conjectures and assumptions.

title: Pauli Propagation For Imaginary-time Evolution
authors: Rafael Gómez-Lurbe And Armando Pérez
abstract: We extend the Pauli propagation framework to imaginary-time evolution and introduce imaginary-time Pauli propagation (ITPP), an operator-based algorithm for approximating thermal and ground-state properties directly in the Pauli basis. We derive explicit imaginary-time propagation rules for Pauli strings and analyze the main approximation errors arising from Trotterization and Pauli-space truncation, including bounds that account for the non-unitary nature of the evolution. Benchmarking ITPP on the one-dimensional transverse field Ising model, we find that the method performs best in the high-temperature regime, where thermal states admit a compressed Pauli-basis approximation, while the required number of Pauli terms grows rapidly as the system approaches the ground-state limit. We further compare with tensor network simulations and study finite-temperature scalability through the number of retained Pauli terms required to reach a fixed target accuracy. These results establish ITPP as a complementary framework for imaginary-time simulation and suggest that combining imaginary-time and real-time Pauli propagation could provide a pathway toward simulating more general non-unitary and open quantum system dynamics within a unified Pauli-based framework.
tldr: The paper introduces imaginary-time Pauli propagation (ITPP), an operator-based algorithm for approximating thermal and ground-state properties in the Pauli basis, benchmarking on the 1D transverse field Ising model.
motivation: To extend the Pauli propagation framework to imaginary-time evolution, providing an alternative method for simulating thermal and ground-state properties that may combine with real-time propagation for broader quantum dynamics.
method: They derive explicit imaginary-time propagation rules for Pauli strings, analyze errors from Trotterization and Pauli-space truncation (accounting for non-unitary evolution), and benchmark on the transverse field Ising model, comparing with tensor network simulations.
result: ITPP performs best in the high-temperature regime where Pauli-basis approximations are compressed, but the number of required Pauli terms grows rapidly near the ground state, limiting scalability to low temperatures.
conclusion: ITPP is a complementary framework for imaginary-time simulation and suggests potential for unified Pauli-based simulation of non-unitary and open quantum systems when combined with real-time propagation.

title: Bound States In The Continuum In Plasmonic Structures
authors: Yao Liang, Sergey Lepeshov, Kirill Koshelev, Andrey Bogdanov, Din Ping Tsai And Yuri Kivshar
abstract: In recent years, increasing attention has been paid to resonant effects in subwavelength photonic systems governed by the physics of bound states in the continuum (BIC). Usually, the resonant effects are associated with low-loss dielectric structures such as metasurfaces. However, BIC is a general wave phenomenon that should be observed in many different systems, including the metal–dielectric structures supporting surface plasmon polaritons, where optical resonances are hindered by losses. This concept provides novel tools for creating sharp resonances in plasmonic nanostructures. Here, we summarize the recent progress in both theoretical and experimental studies of plasmonic BIC with a particular focus on novel properties and applications such as lasing, sensing, and nonlinear properties. In particular, we reveal that plasmonic surface lattice resonances, a metamaterial analog of electromagnetically induced transparency, and Tamm plasmon polaritons can be closely associated with the physics of BIC. In addition, we discuss the future opportunities for the study of high- resonant plasmonic systems with BIC and highlight related areas where they can contribute to novel physics and important applications.
tldr: A review of bound states in the continuum (BIC) in plasmonic structures, discussing theory, experiments, and applications such as lasing and sensing.
motivation: To highlight how BIC physics can create sharp resonances in lossy plasmonic systems, offering novel tools for nanophotonics.
method: Summarizes recent theoretical and experimental progress, connecting plasmonic surface lattice resonances, electromagnetically induced transparency analogs, and Tamm plasmon polaritons to BIC.
result: Shows that BIC can be realized in plasmonic nanostructures, enabling high-Q resonances with potential in lasing, sensing, and nonlinear optics.
conclusion: BIC provides a promising avenue for high-resolution plasmonic resonances, with future opportunities in novel physics and applications.

title: Emergent Symmetry-protected Topological Phases Via Polyakov Confinement In Quantum Spin Systems
authors: Shun-Li Yu And Jian-Xin Li Li-Wei He
abstract: A main theme in modern condensed matter physics is the emergence of fractionalized excitations and gauge structures from quantum spin systems. However, understanding how these exotic degrees of freedom reconfine into new phases of matter remains a fundamental challenge. In this work, we demonstrate that Polyakov’s confinement mechanism-a foundation of compact gauge theory-can serve as a dynamical engine to transform a Dirac spin liquid (DSL) into a symmetry-protected topological (SPT) state. Starting with a DSL with spin-dependent gauge fluxes, we show that the single-occupancy constraint inherent to the physical Hilbert space triggers monopole condensation, dynamically confining bulk spinons while preserving gapless edge modes-realizing a spinon analog of the quantum spin Hall effect. Using a large-scale variational Monte Carlo simulation on a triangular antiferromagnet with an additional Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction, we provide microscopic evidence for this confined SPT phase, including a characteristic area law for the Wilson loop and vanishing topological entanglement entropy. Furthermore, we identify a measurable spin-pump response under magnetic fields, which directly encodes the Berry curvature of the parent Dirac cones. Our results reveal a previously unexplored pathway to SPT physics, bridging the fields of gauge theory, quantum magnetism, and topological matter.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that Polyakov confinement can transform a Dirac spin liquid into a symmetry-protected topological state in quantum spin systems.
motivation: To understand how fractionalized excitations and gauge structures reconfine into new phases of matter, specifically SPT phases.
method: Using large-scale variational Monte Carlo simulation on a triangular antiferromagnet with Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction, they show monopole condensation and spinon confinement.
result: They find a confined SPT phase with area law for Wilson loop and vanishing topological entanglement entropy, and a measurable spin-pump response.
conclusion: They reveal a new pathway to SPT physics via gauge theory and quantum magnetism.

title: Moiré-driven Skyrmion Family
authors: Kuan He, Meng-Han Li, Shi-Da Fan, Zi-Bin Lin, Xiao-Ying Zhuang, Cheng-Lin Han, Li-Qun Chen, Zhao-Dong Xu, Xue-Feng Zhu And Tian-Zhi Yang
abstract: Skyrmion family members, including skyrmions, merons, and skyrmioniums, have been observed in diverse physical systems, yet their coexistence and transformation within a single controllable platform remain challenging. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a bilayer twisted moiré elastic system that enables the generation of multiple skyrmion family members with different topological charges. By constructing three-dimensional displacement vector fields, we establish a framework describing the evolution of topological invariants under twist-induced symmetry modulation, thereby governing controlled transitions and the stable coexistence of different skyrmion textures. In addition, manipulating the Lamb-wave phase introduces discontinuous transport of the topological textures, thereby revealing phason-like dynamics within the quasiperiodic structure. Together, these results provide a versatile route for controlling topological textures and open new possibilities for the design of integrated topological wave devices.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a bilayer twisted moiré elastic system that supports multiple skyrmion family members with controllable topological charges and phason-like dynamics.
motivation: The coexistence and transformation of different skyrmion textures (skyrmions, merons, skyrmioniums) within a single platform has been challenging; the authors aim to provide a controllable system.
method: They construct three-dimensional displacement vector fields in a bilayer twisted moiré elastic system, manipulate Lamb-wave phase, and experimentally demonstrate the topological textures.
result: They achieve simultaneous generation and stable coexistence of multiple skyrmion family members with different topological charges, and reveal discontinuous transport of topological textures.
conclusion: This work offers a versatile route for controlling topological textures in elastic systems, potentially enabling integrated topological wave devices.

title: On The Quantum Computational Complexity Of Classical Linear Dynamics With Geometrically Local Interactions: Dequantization And Universality
authors: Kazuki Sakamoto And Keisuke Fujii
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2182 (2026).

The simulation of large-scale classical systems in exponentially small space on quantum computers has gained attention. The prior work demonstrated that a quantum algorithm offers an exponential speedup over any classical algorithm in simulating classical dynamics with long-range interactions. However, many real-world classical systems, such as those arising from partial differential equations, exhibit only local interactions. The question remains whether quantum algorithms can still provide exponential speedup under this condition. In this work, we thoroughly characterize the computational complexity of simulating such geometrically local systems on quantum computers. First, we dequantize the quantum algorithm for simulating short-time (polynomial-time) dynamics of such systems. This implies that the problem of simulating this dynamics does not yield any exponential quantum advantage. Second, we show that simulating short-time dynamics is at least as hard as polynomial-time and linear-space probabilistic classical computation. Third, we show that the computational complexity of simulating long-time (exponential-time) dynamics is captured by exponential-time and polynomial-space quantum computation. This suggests a super-polynomial time advantage when restricting the computation to polynomial-space, or an exponential space advantage otherwise. This work offers new insights into the complexity of classical dynamics governed by partial differential equations, providing a pathway for achieving quantum advantage in practical problems.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the computational complexity of simulating classical linear dynamics with geometrically local interactions on quantum computers, showing no exponential speedup for short-time dynamics but potential super-polynomial advantages for long-time dynamics under specific computational constraints.
motivation: To determine whether quantum computers can provide exponential speedup for simulating classical systems with local interactions, which are common in partial differential equations, unlike previous work that focused on long-range interactions.
method: The authors dequantize the quantum algorithm for short-time dynamics, prove that simulating short-time dynamics is at least as hard as polynomial-time and linear-space probabilistic classical computation, and analyze long-time dynamics complexity in terms of exponential-time and polynomial-space quantum computation.
result: Short-time dynamics simulation does not yield exponential quantum advantage, while long-time dynamics may offer super-polynomial time advantage under polynomial-space restriction or exponential space advantage otherwise.
conclusion: The work provides new insights into the computational complexity of classical dynamics governed by partial differential equations and identifies conditions where quantum advantage could be achieved.

title: Topology Of non-Hermitian 1d And 2d Su–Schrieffer–Heeger Models: Symmetry Protected Edge And Corner Topological States, non-Hermitian Skin Effect, And Their Interplay
authors: Adrian Pena
abstract: We theoretically investigate the topology of non-Hermitian 1D and 2D Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) models, where non-Hermiticity is introduced through two mechanisms: (i) balanced gain–loss potentials and (ii) nonreciprocal hopping. Our aim is to clarify the interplay between symmetry protected topology, inherited from the Hermitian SSH model, and the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE). For the gain–loss configuration, under periodic boundary conditions (PBC), we identify spectral regimes with purely real, purely imaginary, or mixed eigenvalues. Under open boundary conditions (OBC), two purely imaginary states emerge as exponentially localized edge modes. Through a similarity transformation, we map the model onto a renormalized Hermitian SSH Hamiltonian, demonstrating that these states are the non-Hermitian counterparts of the chiral symmetry protected zero modes of the Hermitian chain. In the 2D extension, we show that mirror symmetry, or its breaking, controls the spatial distribution of topological edge and corner states. For the nonreciprocal hopping model, the PBC complex spectrum forms loops in the complex plane, signaling NHSE together with surviving chiral symmetry protected topology. Using the generalized Brillouin zone (GBZ) formalism and the spectral winding number, we establish a direct relation between hopping nonreciprocity and the left/right accumulation of eigenstates. Under OBC, chiral symmetry protected zero modes appear even in parameter regimes where the Hermitian counterpart is topologically trivial. By continuously deforming the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian into its Hermitian limit, we derive the transition condition into the NHSE phase, consistent with GBZ and spectral winding approaches. In the 2D lattice, the nonreciprocal hopping pattern determines preferential corner localization through a second-order NHSE, in agreement with 1D predictions. We further demonstrate the coexistence of chiral and mirror symmetry protected second-order topology with NHSE.
tldr: The paper theoretically investigates non-Hermitian Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) models in 1D and 2D, exploring symmetry-protected edge and corner states and their interplay with the non-Hermitian skin effect.
motivation: To clarify how non-Hermiticity (via gain–loss and nonreciprocal hopping) affects topological properties inherited from the Hermitian SSH model and to understand the role of the non-Hermitian skin effect in these systems.
method: The authors use two mechanisms to introduce non-Hermiticity, apply similarity transformations to map models onto renormalized Hermitian counterparts, and employ generalized Brillouin zone (GBZ) formalism and spectral winding numbers to analyze topology and skin effect.
result: They identify spectral regimes under periodic boundary conditions, show emergence of exponentially localized edge modes under open boundary conditions, establish a direct relation between hopping nonreciprocity and eigenstate accumulation, and demonstrate coexistence of chiral and mirror symmetry protected second-order topology with the skin effect in 2D.
conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive understanding of topology in non-Hermitian SSH models, highlighting the interplay between symmetry and non-Hermitian effects, but it remains within condensed matter physics without direct connection to the user's specified research directions.

title: New Physics Opportunities At Neutrino Facilities: Bsm Physics At Accelerator, Atmospheric, And Reactor Neutrino Experiments
authors: Koun Choi, Doojin Kim, Jong-Chul Park, Seodong Shin, Pouya Bakhti, Ki-Young Choi, Chang Hyon Ha, Kazumi Hata, Wooyoung Jang, Yu Seon Jeong, Young Ju Ko, Hyun Su Lee, Weijun Li, Yu-Feng Li, Mehedi Masud, Kenny C Y Ng, Jungsic Park, Min-Gwa Park, Komninos-John Plows, Meshkat Rajaee, Eunil Won, Byeongsu Yang, Seong Moon Yoo, Jaehoon Yu And Seokhoon Yun
abstract: Since the discovery of the Higgs boson, the long-standing task at hand in particle physics is the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM), which accounts for only about 5% of the Universe. In light of this situation, the neutrino sector has drawn significant attention due to neutrino oscillations, which require physics BSM and have prompted a wide array of active and planned experimental programs. Notably, neutrino facilities offer substantial potential to search for new physics beyond neutrino oscillations, owing to their precision measurement capabilities, diverse experimental configurations, and various neutrino sources. This white paper summarizes the landscape of new physics that can be probed at current and future neutrino experiments, categorized into laboratory-produced and cosmogenic signals. We discuss recent experimental results interpreted through the lens of new physics, as well as detailed plans and projected sensitivities of next-generation facilities. This summary is based on presentations from the 4th Workshop on New Physics Opportunities in Neutrino Facilities, the 4th Workshop on New Physics Opportunities at Neutrino Facilities (NPN 2024), held at Institute for Basic Science in Daejeon, Korea, on 3–5, June 2024. Particular emphasis is placed on accelerator-based neutrino experiments and a range of neutrino programs in East Asia. We also outline key tasks necessary to realize the promising new physics opportunities ahead.
tldr: A white paper summarizing the landscape of beyond Standard Model (BSM) physics searches possible at current and future neutrino facilities, covering accelerator, atmospheric, and reactor experiments.
motivation: The paper addresses the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model, motivated by the existence of neutrino oscillations which require BSM physics, and aims to consolidate opportunities across neutrino experiment types.
method: It synthesizes presentations from a 2024 workshop, categorizing new physics signals into laboratory-produced and cosmogenic, and discusses recent results and projected sensitivities of next-generation facilities.
result: The paper outlines promising new physics avenues in neutrino experiments, particularly emphasizing accelerator-based and East Asian programs, and identifies key tasks to realize these opportunities.
conclusion: Neutrino facilities offer substantial potential for BSM discoveries, and coordinated efforts in the community are needed to fully exploit them.

title: Review For Stokes-vector And Mueller-matrix Polarization Imaging Technology: Principles, Implementation And Applications
authors: Nan Wang, Houxin Fan, Quanzhou Long And Sailing He
abstract: This review systematically summarizes the principles, technological advancements, and diverse applications of Stokes-vector and Mueller-matrix polarization imaging (PI). The polarization of light is a fundamental property that provides unique and valuable information about the interaction between light and matter. While traditional polarimetry is limited to point-by-point measurements, PI captures the polarization state in a two-dimensional scene, generating a spatial map of parameters for complex and heterogeneous systems. The Stokes–Mueller formalism is the only complete mathematical tool for polarization analysis, using the Stokes vector to describe the light’s state and the Mueller matrix as the transfer function to fully characterize the polarization-altering properties of any medium, including complex depolarizing tissues. The evolution of PI from time-sequential to snapshot paradigms represents a pivotal shift, driven by the pressing need for real-time, motion-artifact-free characterization of dynamic systems. While time-sequential systems laid the foundational framework, their inherent trade-off between acquisition speed and polarization completeness has spurred intense innovation in snapshot methodologies. This transition is not merely a technical improvement but a fundamental enabler for applying polarization analysis to in vivo biological processes and real-time industrial inspection. Applications of PI are wide-ranging, including label-free diagnostics for cancer detection, non-destructive analysis of anisotropic materials, polarization-enhanced target detection, and so on. A future direction is the convergence of PI with hyperspectral detection to form ‘hyper-Stokes/Mueller imaging,’ which promises unprecedented specificity and real-time capability.
tldr: A systematic review of Stokes-vector and Mueller-matrix polarization imaging, covering principles, technological evolution, and applications.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive summary of polarization imaging technology, its development from time-sequential to snapshot methods, and its wide range of applications.
method: The review systematically organizes the principles, implementation techniques, and applications of polarization imaging using Stokes vectors and Mueller matrices.
result: The paper describes the transition to snapshot imaging, lists numerous applications such as cancer diagnosis and material analysis, and proposes future directions like hyperpolarization imaging.
conclusion: Polarization imaging is a powerful tool, and its integration with hyperspectral detection promises enhanced capabilities.

title: The Paradox Of Steady-state Light Diffusion
authors: André Liemert, Lorenzo Pattelli, Alwin Kienle, Federico Tommasi And Fabrizio Martelli
abstract: For over thirty years, the definition of the diffusion coefficient in light transport has been the subject of persistent debate. Its canonical expression includes an explicit dependence on absorption, violating a fundamental scaling property of the radiative transfer equation (RTE). In the time domain (TD), evidence shows that the correct definition is independent of absorption, yet absorption-dependent formulations unfortunately remain common in practical data analysis. In the continuous-wave regime, the radial decay of the RTE can be reproduced by an absorption-dependent coefficient, but this does not imply that steady-state transport is genuinely diffusive. Here, this controversy is resolved through an exact consistency test based solely on the requirement that diffusion converges to the RTE in the limit of infinite propagation. In the TD, we prove that the absorption-independent coefficient is both necessary and sufficient for exact long-time convergence. In the continuous-wave regime, we prove analytically that no scalar diffusion coefficient can make diffusion asymptotically equivalent to the RTE when absorption is nonzero: matching the dominant attenuation length fixes one coefficient, whereas matching the residue requires a different one. We further show that this failure is not caused by any finite set of ballistic or few-scattering contributions, and quantify the intrinsic error introduced by incorrect parameterizations in idealized absorption-retrieval scenarios. These results establish the time-domain formulation as the only self-consistent reference and call for a re-examination of how diffusion is applied in optical transport studies.
tldr: The paper resolves the controversy of absorption-dependent diffusion coefficients in light transport, proving that only in the time domain is the diffusion approximation self-consistent, while in continuous-wave regime no scalar diffusion coefficient can match the radiative transfer equation asymptotically.
motivation: The definition of the diffusion coefficient in light transport has been debated for decades, with absorption-dependent forms violating scaling, and the need to resolve the controversy.
method: The authors use an exact consistency test based on the convergence of diffusion to the radiative transfer equation in the limit of infinite propagation, analyzing both time-domain and continuous-wave regimes analytically.
result: In the time domain, the absorption-independent coefficient is necessary and sufficient for exact long-time convergence; in continuous-wave, no scalar diffusion coefficient can make diffusion asymptotically equivalent to the RTE when absorption is nonzero.
conclusion: The time-domain formulation is the only self-consistent reference, calling for re-examination of diffusion application in optical transport.

title: Probing Quark Electromagnetic Properties Via Entangled Quark Pairs In Fragmentation Hadrons At Lepton Colliders
authors: Qing-Hong Cao, Guanghui Li, Xin-Kai Wen And Bin Yan
abstract: Electromagnetic dipole interactions of light quarks induce distinct spin correlations in quark pairs produced at lepton colliders, favoring entangled spin-triplet state aligned along the axis or spin-singlet state. These correlations lead to unique azimuthal asymmetries in inclusive -dihadron pair production and in back-to-back hadron pairs ( ), which are absent in the SM. Using published Belle and BaBar measurements together with projected sensitivities based on ratios of azimuthal asymmetries, we demonstrate that these measurements provide significant constraints on light-quark dipole couplings, with a reduced dependence on poorly known nonperturbative fragmentation functions and free from contamination by other new physics effects. This approach offers a clean and novel probe of light-quark dipole interactions in collider experiments.
tldr: This paper proposes a new collider probe of light-quark electromagnetic dipole moments using entangled quark pairs and azimuthal asymmetries in dihadron production, constraining dipole couplings with Belle/BaBar data.
motivation: To provide a clean and novel method to probe light-quark dipole interactions, reducing dependence on fragmentation functions and avoiding contamination from other new physics effects.
method: The authors analyze spin correlations in quark pairs produced at lepton colliders, which lead to distinct azimuthal asymmetries in inclusive dihadron and back-to-back hadron pair production. They use published Belle and BaBar measurements and projected sensitivities.
result: The measurements provide significant constraints on light-quark dipole couplings, with reduced dependence on nonperturbative fragmentation functions and free from other new physics contamination.
conclusion: This approach offers a clean and novel probe of light-quark dipole interactions in collider experiments.

title: Activation In Vesicle-mediated Signaling Shaped By Batch Arrival Statistics
authors: Julian B Voits And Ulrich S Schwarz Jan Hauke
abstract: Vesicle-mediated secretion of ions or molecules is a central mechanism of cellular communication, for example in processes such as neurotransmission or hormone release. These events are inherently stochastic: vesicle fusions lead to bursts of variable sizes, releasing discrete packets of transmitters that are subsequently cleared or degraded. The dynamics are intrinsically time-directed due to the interplay of spontaneous bursts and continuous degradation. Using generating functions and a recursion relation, we derive an exact solution for the full time-dependent probability distribution of a general batch arrival-degradation model. This framework also enables a full analysis of first-passage times to a concentration threshold representing downstream activation. We show that activation kinetics are not determined by mean dynamics alone, but depend sensitively on the temporal statistics of arrival events, batch-size variability, and degradation. In particular, different arrival processes with identical mean rates can lead to qualitatively distinct first-passage behavior, reflecting the role of time-asymmetric fluctuations. We also discuss extensions incorporating vesicle depletion. Our results provide a transparent link between stochastic release dynamics and activation timing in vesicle-mediated signaling.
tldr: This paper develops a stochastic model for vesicle-mediated signaling, focusing on how batch arrival statistics and degradation affect activation timing.
motivation: Understanding the stochastic nature of vesicle release is crucial for cellular communication; the authors aim to link release dynamics to downstream activation.
method: They use generating functions and recursion relations to derive exact time-dependent probability distributions for a batch arrival-degradation model and analyze first-passage times.
result: Activation kinetics depend sensitively on the temporal statistics of arrivals, batch-size variability, and degradation, even when mean rates are identical.
conclusion: The results provide a transparent link between stochastic release dynamics and activation timing, with extensions to vesicle depletion.

title: Energy-centric Consumer-resource Theory
authors: Mohammad Salahshour
abstract: Persistent discrepancies between population-growth models and empirical patterns highlight limitations in how classical single-species and consumer-resource models connect population dynamics to macroecological patterns. Here, we develop an energy-centric consumer-resource theory that treats recruitment as constrained by resource influx, while population losses, including those due to predation in the coarse-grained description, are represented as linear losses. This energy-centric approach links some emergent macroecological patterns to the underlying microscopic populations’ fractal distribution and can yield a common von Bertalanffy-like population-dynamic form across trophic levels when fractal scaling holds. Furthermore, we show, within this framework, that energy conservation along the food web gradient naturally leads to a broad range of ecological scaling laws, such as the scaling of biomass production with biomass and the scaling of biomass with primary productivity across trophic levels.
tldr: The paper develops an energy-centric consumer-resource theory linking population dynamics to macroecological patterns and deriving ecological scaling laws.
motivation: Classical population-growth models show persistent discrepancies with empirical patterns, motivating a new theoretical approach.
method: Recruitment is modeled as constrained by resource influx with linear losses, and energy conservation is applied along the food web gradient.
result: Macroecological patterns are linked to fractal population distributions, yielding a common von Bertalanffy-like population-dynamic form and scaling laws for biomass production and biomass with primary productivity.
conclusion: Energy conservation naturally leads to a broad range of ecological scaling laws across trophic levels.

abstract: This review explores different colloidal systems and their crystals as well as their special case namely—mesocrystals. First, we highlight recent advances in fabrication methods of colloidal crystals (mesocrystals) and then describe small-angle and ultra-small-angle x-ray scattering from colloidal assemblies organized from particles of different shape. Here, we already introduce different types of defects that are present in colloidal crystals. Next, we go to a modern description of angular x-ray cross-correlation analysis and its applications on colloidal and mesocrystalline materials. After that we discuss phase retrieval techniques, namely coherent x-ray diffraction imaging and ptychography, as emerging tools for structural characterization of colloidal crystals and mesocrystals. We conclude with perspectives on the opportunities that will be provided by the 4th generation synchrotron sources for studying colloidal crystals and mesocrystals.
tldr: A review of modern X-ray synchrotron methods, including small-angle scattering and coherent imaging, for characterizing colloidal crystals and mesocrystals.
motivation: To provide an overview of advanced structural characterization techniques for colloidal assemblies and their defects.
method: The paper reviews fabrication methods, small-angle and ultra-small-angle X-ray scattering, angular cross-correlation analysis, coherent X-ray diffraction imaging, and ptychography.
result: It summarizes current capabilities and applications of these techniques to colloidal crystals and mesocrystals, highlighting defect analysis and future opportunities.
conclusion: Fourth-generation synchrotron sources will offer enhanced capabilities for studying these materials.

title: Tailoring Reflectionless Complex Media For non-Abelian Braiding Of Acoustic Modes
authors: Hongkuan Zhang And Guancong Ma
abstract: Multiple scattering of sound and light can be tailored for diverse applications. Despite the great progress enabled by technologies such as time-reversal propagation and wavefront shaping, the full control of the transmission matrix remains a significant challenge. In this work, we propose a multi-scattering-based approach to design reflectionless complex media with an arbitrary unitary transmission matrix. As such, the perfect transmission of waves through such a medium performs a unitary operation. Based on this principle, we experimentally demonstrated braiding of multiple waveguide modes in an acoustic waveguide via multiple scattering and showed non-Abelian characteristics arising from the concatenation of distinct complex media. Furthermore, we show that the principle can be extended for realizing arbitrary unitary operations beyond braiding. Our scheme uses generalized Wigner–Smith operators to design the optimal acoustic complex media with near-arbitrary targeted functionalities. The scheme is generally applicable beyond acoustics, with broad implications to other wave types. Our results demonstrate unprecedented control over multiple-scattering waves and establish complex media as a viable route to modal control and operations on compact platforms, providing a new design paradigm for multimode, reconfigurable wave-based devices with potential applications in multiplexed communication, imaging, and the manipulation of quantum waves.
tldr: This paper proposes a method to design reflectionless complex media for arbitrary unitary transmission matrices, experimentally demonstrating non-Abelian braiding of acoustic waveguide modes.
motivation: Achieving full control of the transmission matrix in multiple-scattering systems is challenging; this work aims to enable arbitrary unitary operations on transmitted waves.
method: The authors use generalized Wigner–Smith operators to design optimal acoustic complex media that achieve targeted unitary transmission matrices.
result: They experimentally demonstrated braiding of multiple waveguide modes in an acoustic waveguide, revealing non-Abelian characteristics when concatenating distinct media.
conclusion: The scheme extends beyond acoustics and offers a new paradigm for designing multimode, reconfigurable wave-based devices with potential applications in communication, imaging, and quantum wave manipulation.
